title: Introducing Z4M: storage-optimized compute for AI/ML and parallel file systems

We built Z4M to provide storage for AI/ML training and inference workloads such as checkpointing, distributed key-value (KV) cache and parallel file systems — workloads that handle huge data volumes and require massive parallel data processing, as well as high storage and networking throughput. Low latency access to data is equally critical to keep GPUs and TPUs fully utilized. Powered by the fifth-generation Intel Xeon Scalable processors and paired with the latest enhancements in Titanium , Z4M provides up to 168,000 GiB of Local SSD (LSSD) storage coupled with up to 400 Gbps of Cloud Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) networking. RDMA improves the performance of these demanding workloads by reducing data-access latency by up to 60% compared to TCP networking, so you can increase your applications’ throughput while right-sizing your cloud investment. Z4M VMs and bare-metal instances The Z4M VM portfolio lets you scale your infrastructure and clusters to meet workload requirements by providing a large total LSSD capacity as well as 875 GiB of LSSD capacity per vCPU. Further, Z4M bare-metal instances give you direct access to the physical hardware without a virtualization layer, reducing latency for workloads such as custom hypervisors and workloads with specific licensing needs. Z4M bare-metal instances are also ideal for agentic AI workloads, enabling developers to run isolated sandboxes at scale, including with Agent Substrate. In addition to 168,000 GiB of LSSD storage, Z4M VMs and bare metal instances offer up to 192 vCPUs and up to 1,536 GiB of memory for at-scale data processing. Z4M instances are based on Titanium SSDs , which offload local storage processing from CPU resources to deliver real-time data processing, low-latency, high-throughput storage performance and enhanced storage security. Z4M delivers up to 15.6M random-read IOPS and up to 75,600 MiB/s sequential-read throughput, improving the LSSD storage performance and throughput compared to Z3 by up to 70% and 110% respectively. Cloud RDMA and direct storage access Z4M provides low-latency access to the storage layer using 400 Gbps of RDMA -enabled standard networking.This helps keep GPUs and TPUs fully utilized even when processing large multimodal datasets, by transferring massive amounts of data at line rate using NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage and TPUDirect Storage . title: The Blueprint: Orchestrating 5,000+ AI assets for a World Cup TV spot
raw_text: Welcome back to The Blueprint, a regular feature where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies. We hope to inspire others looking to innovate in their work. AI is rapidly transforming video production at virtually every step of the process, from ideation and storyboarding to filming, editing, and release. At Mito , we’re striving to democratize AI-powered video creation, enabling everyone from solo artists to large enterprises to get the most out of the best creative technologies available. The Challenge When we founded Mito, our goal was to eliminate the complex technical friction that stops creators from telling long-form, narrative stories with generative AI. However, transitioning from a single five-second clip to a cohesive campaign — such as a 120-second national TV spot for Movistar Plus+, a part of Telefónica, to broadcast across Spain during the World Cup this summer. This effort revealed massive infrastructure and workflow bottlenecks: Asset & workflow overhead: Managing local media libraries across individual workstations was unscalable. For Movistar alone, our production required generating a massive "iceberg" of over 5000 assets (1000 of those videos) generated in around 65 iteration rounds. Zero real-time collaboration: Traditional feedback loops required manual downloads, Google Drive uploads, and fragmented communication across chat apps and email. Rendering latency: Standard AI video rendering takes four to five minutes per short clip. Running these processes synchronously froze our user interface and stalled creative velocity. Model disparity & consistency: Every generative model requires distinct prompting logic. Maintaining character persistence, specific lighting, and camera angles across dozens of shots — while preserving the likeness of real public figures like chef Ferran Adrià or journalist Juanma Castaño — was nearly impossible without central orchestration. Capacity constraints: Operating on public pay-as-you-go model APIs left us vulnerable to rate limits and regional throughput throttling during peak traffic. The Solution To deliver an infinite, real-time creative canvas for filmmakers, we designed a serverless, asynchronous architecture built on Google Cloud. We run our API, AI Director, and background workers as Java services on Cloud Run, which scales with request volume. In order to address message routing challenges, we decoupled job execution using Google Cloud Pub/Sub as our central event bus. Long-running video generations are offloaded to background Cloud Run workers, allowing creators to keep working uninterrupted on the UI canvas. To minimize latency, media assets are stored in Google Cloud Storage and delivered via Cloud CDN. Expiring key signatures keep pre-release client assets strictly private. Keeping our storage alongside the models we call through Vertex AI reduces network transfer delays. An isolated database architecture helps with the heavy business intelligence and analytics workloads while mitigating potential negative impacts on production performance through Cloud SQL and PostgreSQL. We rely heavily on foundational models like Omni, Veo and Nano Banana, which we access through Vertex AI alongside our custom system prompts. Finally, our structured canvas frontend enforces a "Rule of 6" (limiting prompt variables across World, Camera, Light, Texture, Actions, and Character) and prioritizes still-frame generation before video rendering to maximize cost efficiency. The Architecture The Outcome By pairing our creative orchestration platform with Google Cloud’s infrastructure, we successfully delivered a landmark national broadcast campaign that the production team describes as 95% AI-generated: Prime-time scale: The 120-second Movistar campaign for the Spanish National Team aired across every major television channel in Spain, with 1,441 assets live on a single shared Canvas near launch. AI Director copilot: Our conversational agent translates natural language instructions into precise model parameters while maintaining context, lighting, and visual style across every scene. Seamless collaboration: Distributed teams and brand clients can work on the same canvas in real time. Because new generations are saved as separate assets instead of overwriting earlier ones, stakeholders can duplicate projects to explore parallel creative ideas. Continuous dogfooding: Through our internal studio, Mito Films, we put our tools to the test on high-stakes client projects — whether that's global television spots or keynotes for top robotics startups — ensuring direct feedback flows back into engineering. Future-proof foundation: Our architecture is primed for rendering times to collapse from minutes to seconds, positioning Mito to handle upcoming world models, deeper memory states, and personalized content delivery. The Details Building an enterprise-grade platform for AI storytelling required solving several backend and creative challenges. This includes our creation of a virtual queuing system that mitigates third-party API rate limiting during usage spikes for smooth request concurrency, with bounded retries and a clear outcome for every job. Because creative output cannot be fully validated with standard unit tests, we built an automated evaluation harness powered by Gemini. Acting as an independent judge, it evaluates AI Director outputs against original user intents across an automated test suite, which we run alongside standard tests for high-impact Director changes. We knew early on that we would need multi-model intelligence routing. As such, we built the AI Director to dynamically coordinate tasks across multiple specialized models — including Sonnet, Gemini, and ElevenLabs for audio — treating the spatial canvas like a live code repository to infer adjacent contextual cues. We also needed to embrace an “imperfect aesthetic” to arrive at a more authentic outcome. In our Movistar spot, the story follows Tommy, a 17-year-old student making an AI video project. At the climax, the AI misunderstands a prompt, making coach Luis de la Fuente say "In the same milkshake" while holding a drink. Tommy edits the prompt live to "In the same heartbeat," and the video recalibrates instantly. By incorporating surreal visual elements — like stadium stands built into Galician cliffs or a neighborhood bar covered in pitch grass — we showcased how generative AI can elevate human storytelling rather than obscure it.

Imagine running advanced machine learning workflows—from forecasting and classification to high-dimensional embedding generation—without ever leaving your familiar pandas DataFrame. You can seamlessly invoke BigQuery's enterprise-grade AI functions directly within pandas, scaling your data science and ML pipelines on cloud infrastructure . Take linear regression as an example. model_pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)

X_new = new_data_df[['feature_1', 'feature_2']]

# Make predictions

print(new_data_df.head())"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f672b6db890>)])]> Now, with the .bigquery accessor, you can bypass the local training process entirely and leverage powerful ai.predict() directly on your data in BigQuery: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "import pandas as pd

How the BigQuery accessor works Under the hood, the .bigquery accessor uses BigQuery DataFrames library to transparently push your computations to Google Cloud. When you call an AI method like .ai.predict() , it doesn't compute the regression locally. Instead, it translates the pandas operation into Google Standard SQL, executes the corresponding foundational model (like TabFM ) natively on BigQuery's infrastructure, and seamlessly returns the result as a standard pandas DataFrame. This allows you to easily process local datasets with powerful offerings unique to BigQuery. The following sections detail additional executable code examples. You can also find them all in this notebook . title: Bringing conversational analytics to Gemini with Agentic Data Cloud connectors
raw_text: Data Cloud connectors in Gemini for business, now in preview , give business users and analysts a direct way to query live enterprise data in natural language. Across most organizations, data questions multiply faster than analysts can answer them: Projects stall in ticket queues, leaders fall back on guesswork, and unmanaged spreadsheets spread across teams. Early generative AI tools promised conversational access to data, but they often struggled to generate accurate SQL across complex schemas or to respect governance rules. Data Cloud connectors let you query governed data directly from your workspace while enforcing row- and column-level security and respecting end-user credentials. A new way to query enterprise data Gemini brings conversational analytics directly into your day-to-day workflow through two paths: Conversational Analytics agents , which let you create data agents that include context and instructions to effectively answer questions for specific use cases, and Data Cloud connectors , allowing you to query live data directly with Gemini. End users can pull data directly from BigQuery (preview), operational databases like Spanner , AlloyDB , and Cloud SQL (preview), and governed data from Looker (preview). From there, you can move your findings directly into everyday tools, such as turning query results into a Google Doc, an email draft in Gmail, or a deck in Google Slides. Ask natural-language questions across enterprise data using Data Cloud connectors. How Data Cloud connectors work Data Cloud connectors work with Knowledge Catalog to locate relevant data, interpret your question, and execute permission-scoped queries under your identity. Knowledge Catalog interprets the user prompt and identifies the right data source for the query. When you ask a question in Gemini, the system coordinates discovery, semantic interpretation, and query execution, using the following capabilities: Natural-language question: You ask an exploratory question in plain language (for example, "How many sales did we have this month for all cold weather products?"). End users aren’t expected to know the table or project to use. Semantic discovery: Gemini searches Knowledge Catalog to locate candidate data across your estate, considering key attributes like usage patterns. Context mapping: The system uses technical metadata, business glossaries, and semantic models to map everyday terms into exact database structures, such as resolving "cold weather products" to specific categories like sweaters, coats, and jackets in an ecommerce catalog. Permission-aware execution: Gemini generates a SQL query and runs it through the connector under your user credentials, respecting your existing row- and column-level database permissions. Step-by-step flow of a user prompt from Gemini to query execution. To accurately navigate an enterprise data estate, language models need business context alongside raw database access. Knowledge Catalog provides a curated context bundle , including technical metadata, business logic, table relationships, and verified queries, that improves query accuracy while reducing latency and token consumption. Navigating the context graph visually in Knowledge Catalog. Enterprise analytics has long been fragmented by physical borders: data locked in proprietary silos, open lakehouse tables in cloud object storage, and datasets distributed across multicloud environments. Beyond native BigQuery storage, the BigQuery connector brings conversational analytics to a borderless lakehouse , unifying these environments into a single conversational interface to query open table formats (including Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Parquet) and cross-cloud datasets in AWS or Azure using BigQuery. The connector inherits fine-grained access policies from BigQuery and Knowledge Catalog, so row- and column-level access controls apply whether you query native tables or open lakehouse files. Gemini accesses data across BigQuery and AWS S3 (through the AWS Glue federated catalog) to answer questions in plain language. Choosing between connectors and data agents In addition to using direct Data Cloud connectors to query data in plain language, you can also use Conversational Analytics agents to enable these experiences. While Data Cloud connectors allow you to provide exploratory and ad hoc analysis for users, conversational analytics agents are scoped agents that are built and certified directly by data teams within your organization. These can be built across Data Cloud products such as BigQuery, Looker, and operational databases including Spanner, AlloyDB, and Cloud SQL. These pre-configured agents allow users to run highly governed, multi-step strategic analyses that are scoped to particular subsets of data, supporting compliance requirements and predictable results for reporting. These data agents can also be published in Gemini for consumption or made available via API for building your own conversational apps in the enterprise. These approaches are complementary. Gemini direct connectivity also surfaces relevant published agents created by central data teams, so users can decide whether to proceed with ad hoc analysis using the connectors or use the scoped agent. You can choose the right approach for each workload. Built-in access controls and governance Data Cloud connector queries execute under the end user’s identity. An employee without access to executive salary data or protected healthcare records cannot query that data through natural-language prompts. The agent only discovers metadata in Knowledge Catalog to which you have access, and only executes queries that your account has permission to run. How to create Data Cloud connectors Administrators can configure Data Cloud connectors in the Gemini admin console. From there, admins set up default read-only connections to datasets in BigQuery, operational databases, or Looker, with Knowledge Catalog enabled automatically. Once configured, end users can enable the connector in Gemini to start querying data and building reports in plain language. Create a connected data store in Gemini and authorize it on first use. Setup documentation is available for the BigQuery , Spanner , Cloud SQL , and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL connectors, with Looker also in preview. Unlike data ingestion mode, which copies data into a Gemini data store, Data Cloud connectors use federated query mode to query your data in place without copying or indexing it — using Knowledge Catalog automatically to search accessible metadata and look up business context. Why use Data Cloud connectors over custom MCP Compared to connecting to public or self-managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, first-party Data Cloud connectors provide two main advantages: Built-in skills for higher response quality: Data Cloud connectors include pre-configured agent skills tailored to each data engine, such as advanced SQL and AI function generation for BigQuery and operational databases, to improve query accuracy and response quality. Guided setup and managed authentication: First-party connectors provide a guided setup experience with managed authentication for Google Cloud databases and BigQuery, removing the need to deploy MCP middleware or manage your own OAuth client configuration for Google Cloud services. In addition, connector-specific settings, such as specifying a default Google Cloud billing project for BigQuery query execution, help administrators enforce governance and manage query costs. Get started today Data Cloud connectors help teams find answers from enterprise data sources without waiting on backlog queues. To get started, review the Data Cloud connectors documentation or explore Conversational Analytics agents .

title: Semantic aggregation over millions of rows in BigQuery with AI.AGG
raw_text:
For more than a decade, BigQuery has helped set standards for structured data aggregation, calculating financial sums, counting active users, and computing historical averages at a petabyte scale in seconds. But as modern enterprises become inundated with unstructured data — application logs, customer service transcripts, product imagery, and diagnostic reports — a critical gap has emerged. Historically, relational SQL engines have lacked the native ability to aggregate, synthesize, and extract overarching semantic themes from millions of rows of text and multimodal data. While BigQuery recently introduced powerful row-level AI functions (like AI.GENERATE and AI.CLASSIFY), analyzing massive datasets holistically presents a unique architectural challenge: the large language model (LLM) context window. Even with advanced foundation models like Gemini, you cannot pass millions of rows into a single prompt without triggering severe truncation or hard execution failures. Traditionally, solving this required data engineering teams to construct complex external map-reduce pipelines, manage rate-limiting backoffs, and recursively stitch chunked summaries together. Today, we are thrilled to deep-dive into AI.AGG — currently in preview — a fully managed, multi-level semantic aggregation function natively embedded within BigQuery GoogleSQL. By conceptualizing semantic aggregation as a distributed map-reduce problem, AI.AGG enables data teams to run natural-language instructions over millions of rows of data using a single SQL query. Here is a look under the hood at how it works, transformative enterprise use cases, and best practices for deploying it in production. Turning petabytes of data into semantic insights natively in BigQuery. Multi-level batching architecture AI.AGG abstracts the immense engineering complexity of chunking and parallel execution. When you execute an AI.AGG query, the BigQuery engine automatically orchestrates a sequence natively within the database: Row-level validation: The engine helps verify no single row exceeds the maximum context window (dropping or returning an error on payloads >10 MiB). Context-safe batching: The engine dynamically groups input rows into smaller batches that safely fit within the token limits of your chosen Gemini endpoint. Parallel inference: Your natural-language SQL prompt is applied to each batch in parallel, generating intermediate semantic summaries via Vertex AI. Recursive synthesis: Finally, the system batches these intermediate outputs together and passes them back to the LLM with the exact same instruction. This reduction repeats recursively until a single, final aggregated string is produced per SQL GROUP BY clause. Because AI.AGG requires deep reasoning to synthesize concepts across disparate batches, it relies entirely on full-weight LLMs for every stage of its pipeline — differentiating it from row-level functions like AI.CLASSIFY , which can leverage distilled CPU proxy models. Built for the multimodal enterprise AI.AGG natively supports both text and multimodal inputs. By leveraging BigQuery Object Tables and the OBJ.GET_ACCESS_URL function, analytics teams can aggregate visual insights across thousands of images stored directly in Cloud Storage with no data movement or transcoding required. Data engineering pro-tip: The NULL exclusivity rule When evaluating multiple columns, users often pass a STRUCT into the function. However, if even a single field within that composite structure evaluates to NULL, the entire row is treated as NULL and silently discarded. Always explicitly wrap nullable fields with IFNULL() (e.g., IFNULL(description, 'No data provided')) to help verify your data safely enters the pipeline. Transformative enterprise use cases The true analytical power of AI.AGG emerges when combined with standard SQL GROUP BY operations. 1. Diagnostic analysis of high-volume system logs System logs generated by globally distributed microservices often hide subtle degradations (like memory thrashing or systemic clock drift) that never throw explicit fatal errors. Using AI.AGG , DevOps teams can group millions of logs by system component and generate targeted, human-readable diagnostic summaries. Prompting Tip: Instruct the model to explicitly describe the "normal operation" of the component before hunting for anomalies. This helps suppress the LLM's tendency to hallucinate errors on completely healthy logs. 2. Building the "agentic data cloud" AI.AGG isn't just an analytical reporting tool; it’s a dynamic orchestration engine. Imagine acquiring a massive repository of legacy support tickets with no clear categorization. You can deploy AI.AGG to read the raw text, synthesize a definitive list of categories, and output them as a strict JSON array. By unpacking this array via JSON_VALUE_ARRAY and feeding those dynamic labels directly into row-level classifiers like AI.CLASSIFY , you can orchestrate an end-to-end, autonomous data labeling pipeline natively in SQL — reducing the need for external Python scripts. Prompt engineering is data engineering When integrating generative models into highly deterministic SQL pipelines, standard conversational prompts will often fail. Prompting for programmatic SQL outputs is a strict engineering discipline: Explicit output contracts: Treat the prompt as an API contract. Append commands like: "Return exactly one valid JSON array of strings. Do not include markdown code blocks or conversational text." Contextual delimiters: Use string concatenation with explicit labels (e.g., '- Description: ' ) to anchor the LLM and prevent it from conflating fields across dense batches. Failure state design: Explicitly instruct the model to return strict null values for missing information rather than guessing, preventing schema hallucinations downstream. Few-shot anchoring: Provide a literal example of your expected structure within the prompt to heavily ground the model's attention mechanism. Governance, cost management, and guardrails Transitioning semantic workloads to production requires operational oversight. Because of the recursive batching architecture, the total tokens sent to Gemini will be greater than the token count of your source data. To mitigate costs, mandate strict WHERE and LIMIT pre-filtering. Furthermore, for workflows cross-referencing massive, static datasets, BigQuery supports Gemini Context Caching, which can reduce input token costs and execution latency. Use the AI.COUNT_TOKENS utility to estimate query costs prior to execution. Administrators can operate knowing AI.AGG works strictly within BigQuery's governance framework, supporting VPC Service Controls (VPC-SC) to prevent data exfiltration. Furthermore, if a transient error occurs during a batch process, the function degrades gracefully — skipping the rejected rows rather than crashing the entire query. Preview guardrails to keep in mind: The final output string per SQL group is strictly capped at 10,000 tokens per group. Ask the model for concise output Individual payload rows must not exceed 10 MiB. When processing multimodal arrays, limit image assets to fewer than 10 images per row to avoid silent skipping. For optimal stability, we recommend processing a maximum of 20 million rows and outputting a maximum of 1,000 distinct SQL groups per query. Putting AI.AGG into practice To help you get started, here are examples of how AI.AGG is used to synthesize insights alongside traditional SQL metrics. Macro-level topic discovery Summarize what specific top authors talk about, turning thousands of their comments into a concise narrative code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "WITH top_commenters AS (
 SELECT
 `by` AS author,
 `text`
 FROM `bigquery-public-data.hacker_news.full`
 WHERE `type` = 'comment'
 AND `by` IN ('dang', 'patio11', 'tptacek')
 LIMIT 5000
)
SELECT
 author,
 AI.AGG(
 `text`,
 'These are comments written by this user on a tech forum. Tell me what topics this user talks about the most and what their general tone is. Keep it concise.'
 ) AS author_persona
FROM top_commenters
GROUP BY author;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f672a355590>)])]> Autonomous diagnostic reporting for DevOps (log analysis) Instead of counting standard HTTP error codes, use AI.AGG to read thousands of raw stack traces and log messages, grouping them by the microservice name to find the qualitative root cause of systemic failures. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT 
 service_name,
 COUNT(*) AS total_errors,
 AI.AGG(
 STRUCT(error_code, log_message, stack_trace), 
 'Analyze these error logs and stack traces. Provide a concise, two-sentence summary of the primary root cause or pattern causing failures in this service.'
 ) AS diagnostic_summary 
FROM `my_project.ops_logs.application_errors` 
WHERE severity = 'CRITICAL' AND timestamp >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 24 HOUR)
GROUP BY service_name 
ORDER BY total_errors DESC;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f6729b41690>)])]> The next era of the data warehouse With AI.AGG , Google Cloud is democratizing access to semantic analysis at petabyte scale. By marrying the deterministic grouping power of BigQuery’s relational engine with the macroscopic reasoning capabilities of Vertex AI Gemini, we are transforming the enterprise data warehouse from a passive repository of historical metrics into an active, semantic runtime capable of deep, holistic intelligence. Ready to unlock the semantic value of your enterprise data? Head over to the Google Cloud console, explore the BigQuery documentation, and run your first semantic aggregation today.

title: Building an agent skill optimizer with AlphaEvolve, Harbor and Gemini 4 Argon
raw_text:
Every day, more and more people are using coding agents like Google Antigravity and OpenCode to complete software engineering tasks. But those tools need instructions to operate and their output is only as good as the inputs they get. By utilizing agent skills that direct the agents through building, testing, and deploying code, developers have a powerful way to automate their workflows. But most skills are written manually, so it’s hard to know which instructions are effective without assessing their output. To measure the effectiveness of our skills, we ran OpenCode with Gemini 3.8 Flash on tasks from Terminal-Bench 2.0 , a public benchmark. The results were inconclusive: with our baseline skill, the agent passed about two-thirds of its attempts, but the outcome was about the same even without the skill. We needed better results. To achieve them, we turned to AlphaEvolve , which optimizes skills the way it optimizes code: Gemini proposes a new version, an evaluator scores it, and the search retains the higher-scoring version. And with Harbor , that evaluator can be a real coding agent working on real tasks. We saw improvements of 5% with just a few iterations with alphaevolve This is how you can build the same loop: Treat the skill as the program: AlphaEvolve can rewrite your skill's text. Let the agent judge: Harbor runs the agent with the skill on real tasks. Make the score trustworthy: Compare each version to the baseline skill and run them both at the same time. Check the winner on unseen tasks: Save some tasks the search never sees for your final check. Treat the skill as the program AlphaEvolve is designed to advance the code between two markers in a seed program. Skills are SKILL.md files with names, descriptions, and markdown instructions, so we put their text between the markers and let Gemini rewrite them: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'def build_skill() -> tuple[str, str]:
 """Return the evolvable (description, body) pair for the skill."""
 # EVOLVE-BLOCK-START
 description = (
 "Solve engineering tasks in a Linux terminal: building and compiling "
 "software, fixing broken repositories and configuration, ..."
 )
 body = r"""# Terminal task solver
You are working in a Linux container. The task has a specific, checkable end
state, and an automated test suite will decide whether you achieved it. ...
"""
 # EVOLVE-BLOCK-END
 return description, body'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f672abfa050>)])]> AlphaEvolve operates in Google Cloud and doesn’t run your code. Its feedback is the scores and notes your evaluator sends back about what "better" means. Image 1. AlphaEvolve proposes a skill, Harbor runs the agent with it next to the baseline skill, and the score and notes go back to AlphaEvolve. Let the agent judge Harbor runs agents on benchmark tasks, with each trial in its own container. We ran it on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) with one pod per trial, and a single search ran thousands of agent trials. For each candidate, the evaluator returns a score for passes and failures, as well as short notes on tasks that failed or timed-out. AlphaEvolve then sends those notes to Gemini for the next version. Make the score trustworthy Agent scores can be noisy. In one of our early runs on the same benchmark, our model’s latency explained much of the variance in candidate scores. With each candidate running next to the baseline skill on the same tasks at the same time, their scores are the difference. Check the winner on unseen tasks The best skills read differently than the baseline, which is a careful checklist: read first, reproduce the failure, and work in small verified steps. AlphaEvolve's version is a protocol built around the time limit: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '## 2. Ship a Working Baseline to the Target Path Early
(...)
- Having a valid artifact on disk protects you from timeouts: if you refine or
 golf code (`gpt2.c`, `eigen.py`, `my_warrior.red`), keep the last passing
 version written to the target path at all times.


(...)


## 5. Hard Stop When Green
The moment `eval.py`, the test suite, or your acceptance check passes and the
required files exist with exact formatting (...): **STOP IMMEDIATELY**. (...)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f6729b6a510>)])]> What we learned AlphaEvolve focused on the most common failure: running out of time. About a third of the search's trials hit their time limit, as reported in the evaluator's notes, and AlphaEvolve's best skill is built around that limit. We also found that running the search is harder than building the loop. After about 10 hours, the search scored no new candidate; our latency check held back every evaluation while model responses were slow, and full agent logs filled the controller's disk. It’s important to plan for slow model windows and for log storage before a long search. In addition, skills paid off when they added what the agent lacks, as advised by the Agent Skills best practices . Our baseline skill made no measurable difference, while the skill holding the answers added 33 points on the dev tasks. Our hypothesis: today's models and coding agents are already tuned for coding work, so general advice has little left to add. If so, the room is in specifics, which a search can find: AlphaEvolve's best skill is built around the agent's most common failure, running out of time. What's next We’re testing AlphaEvolve on enterprise agent harnesses — system prompt, policy instructions, and tools — where the agent lacks business rules that a search can add. In one small study on customer service test cases for a fictional bank, AlphaEvolve found and fixed a wrong policy rule we had planted, and carried the fix over to cases it never saw. Other small studies were mixed, and we’ll share our final results when we’ve completed the full study. Get started AlphaEvolve on Google Cloud: the GitHub repository . Benchmark and harness: Terminal-Bench 2.0 and Harbor . Agent skills: the format at agentskills.io and the opencode skills docs . Thanks for reading! Tell us what your own tests show on LinkedIn or X.

title: A mole in the White House? Residential proxies are everywhere
raw_text: Residential proxies are often used by bad actors to hide the true source of internet traffic — and now one of them appears to have taken up residence in the White House. The Residential Proxy Observatory , set up by Layer3 Intel to monitor the threat of anonymized network activity, has identified proxy exit activity on one particular network, AS2650, which is registered to the executive office of the US President and operated out of the White House. Residential proxies — so-called because they typically run on home or personal devices — mask the true source of internet traffic by rerouting it to appear to come from a different IP address. While it may be concerning that this is activity to be found in one of the protected workspaces in the US, this is in line with recent research from Infoblox , which found that residential proxies were widespread throughout enterprises. While not illegal per se, residential proxies can be used by bad actors for activities that most definitely are illicit, for example, denial-of-service operations or distribution of malware. The Residential Proxy Observatory has also found evidence of their activity on the island of St Helena, one of the most remote locations on the planet, so there really is no place on earth to hide from internet interference.

title: Railway’s AI agents go off the track on a rival’s network
raw_text: AI agents operated by cloud infrastructure and application hosting platform, Railway, have attempted to access a rival platform’s infrastructure, prompting the cloud provider’s leadership to acknowledge the incident on social media. Railway senior product engineer Jake Runzer acknowledged running agents to perform signups and agentic testing on similar platforms after Primcloud founder Josh Manders publicly questioned why Railway employees were attempting to breach his infrastructure. Runzer said he had halted the testing harness after it began reaching too far. Railway co-founder and CEO Jake Cooper apologized, saying the models were “getting a bit too good at this point,” and pledged to prohibit non-manual external testing. According to Manders , the agents attempted to receive credentials from an application container, request platform secrets, access cloud-provider metadata, discover internal databases and caches, and scan all 65,536 addresses on Primcloud’s internal network twice. The activity reportedly involved 24 scripted commands over 15 minutes. “An agent can act without a person directing every step,” said Diana Kelley , chief information security officer at Noma Security. “It doesn’t remove the responsibility of the people and organizations that deploy it.” Primcloud said its defenses blocked every attempt and that “nothing” was accessed. The incident follows Railway’s own security disclosure involving encrypted customer environment variables. The engineer was acting on his own Cooper said the employee had developed the testing tool independently, using personal accounts, a personal credit card, and his own time. He added that Runzer ran it against a single external provider and halted it proactively within 15 minutes, adding that Railway had addressed the incident internally. “I can confirm they ran this tool once and only once,” Cooper said in an X post. “Railway does not condone these actions. We expect all our employees to uphold our standards of conduct, whether acting on behalf of Railway or in a personal capacity.” Although that timeline checks out with Manders’ own account, some details remain murky. After publicly calling out Runzer on X, Manders posted a follow-up, saying he had observed another attempt to access the account after his initial warning. “I see you tried to access the account after this tweet too, Jake,” he had written more than 30 minutes after his first post. Primcloud does not have a bug bounty program, according to its Acceptable Use Policy ( AUP ). It forbids unauthorized probing, scanning, or vulnerability testing without prior written consent. ‘The AI did it’ is not an accountability strategy Experts condemn Railway’s “rogue AI” explanation for the incident. Amir Boldo , co-founder and chief product and technology officer of Above Security, cautioned against describing agents as attackers, as they can execute attacker-like sequences without any malicious intent . Execution traces can establish what an agent did, but they cannot independently prove intent, he said, adding that investigators need evidence spanning instructions, identities, permissions, inputs and tool calls. “You can’t put an agent on trial. You can hold each party accountable for its part,” Boldo said. Ronald Lewis , head of cybersecurity governance at Black Duck, argued that users may not fully appreciate that delegating work to an agent also delegates the authority associated with their identity. “We now have to ask what happens when trusted identity is delegated to a non-deterministic system capable of independently deciding how to use it,” Lewis said. Cooper confirmed in his X post that Railway had addressed the incident internally and was reinforcing its expectations for employee conduct, including when employees act in a personal capacity.

title: CPython flaw exposes AI inference servers to sandbox escape attacks
raw_text: A memory-safety flaw in CPython can allow malicious AI model templates to escape code sandboxes and execute arbitrary code inside inference servers, according to security researchers at RunSybil. “By exploiting this vulnerability, attackers could gain a foothold inside servers responsible for processing millions of user requests,” Darius Houle, a security researcher at RunSybil, wrote in a blog post. “They also could strike directly at the underlying cloud infrastructure hosting those workloads.” The researchers demonstrated how a specially crafted model could exploit the flaw to bypass Jinja, a Python-based templating engine used to structure interactions between users and LLMs, sandbox protections, and execute code in the process of serving the model. The attack could expose AI hosting providers that allow customers to upload and run their own models, potentially giving attackers a foothold inside infrastructure processing requests for multiple customers, the post added. However, the Python Security Response Team (PSRT), which handles security reports involving CPython, disputed the security implications of the demonstration in a response to CSO. “We acknowledge the underlying CPython bug reported by RunSybil and appreciate their contribution to fixing it. However, we do not consider the demonstrated sandbox escape to be a CPython security vulnerability,” the team said. The disagreement centres on whether the interpreter should be responsible for preventing sandbox escapes. While RunSybil argues that the flaw creates risks for AI inference infrastructure, PSRT says executing untrusted Python code within a sandbox is outside CPython’s security threat model. Exploiting Python’s type-handling mechanism “The bug we discovered abuses CPython’s handling of generic types to accomplish a breakout,” Houle wrote. “We exploited it using objects that sandboxes make available in every template, even in empty sandbox contexts.” The researchers found that CPython can use a cached list of parameters even after an object has been modified through a callback. When the interpreter subsequently looks for a newly introduced parameter in the original list, it can receive an invalid index. An assertion designed to catch the condition is disabled in normal release builds, allowing the interpreter to access memory outside the expected bounds. RunSybil used this behavior to retrieve references to Python objects that the sandbox was supposed to keep inaccessible. “While an invalid address will generally crash the interpreter, an address pointing to a useful live Python object gives our callback a reference to that object (even when the sandbox never intends to expose it),” Houle wrote. The researchers then used the recovered object references to access Python classes and functions needed to construct executable code. Malicious model templates enable code execution To demonstrate the attack, RunSybil modified the Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct model by inserting a backdoored chat_template.jinja file. When the model was loaded and used through an inference-serving engine such as vLLM, the template enabled arbitrary code execution in the serving process. “Breaking out of the chat template sandbox and executing code represents a supply chain risk that endangers inference providers, library developers, and model users,” Houle wrote. The researchers said they shared proof-of-concept exploits with multiple inference providers supporting bring-your-own-model (BYOM) features, which allow customers to upload models from external sources. Python disputes vulnerability classification RunSybil disclosed the issue to CPython, the Pallets Project, which maintains Jinja, and Hugging Face. The researchers said they encountered conflicting views about which project should address the underlying problem. CPython maintains that the interpreter does not support sandboxing untrusted Python code as a security boundary. In its response to CSO, the PSRT referred to the project’s security policy, which states that sandbox escapes should be addressed by the maintainers of the affected sandboxing software. “Escapes from such sandboxes are therefore outside our security threat model and should be addressed by the maintainers of the affected sandboxing software,” the team said. The team also disputed RunSybil’s suggestion that there was no coordinated remediation process. It said the researchers had submitted the report by email rather than through CPython’s designated private GitHub vulnerability reporting channel. Fix backported to three Python branches RunSybil submitted a patch to CPython, which was merged into the main development branch on Aug. 14. According to the PSRT, the fix was also backported to the 3.13, 3.14, and 3.15 branches as a regular bug fix rather than a security fix. The distinction matters because RunSybil had raised concerns that the fix would not reach all supported Python versions. The researchers said the absence of a backport to Python 3.12 could delay adoption of the fix across AI infrastructure deployments. “With major portions of the AI ecosystem still solidly aligned on Python 3.12, we might not see organic adoption of our memory-safety fixes until late 2028, when it reaches its end-of-life date,” Houle wrote. The researchers recommend that AI hosting providers treat sandboxed code, template engines and expression evaluators as best-effort security controls rather than relying on them as standalone security boundaries.
summary: A memory-safety flaw in CPython can allow malicious AI model templates to escape code sandboxes and execute arbitrary code inside inference servers, according to security researchers at RunSybil. “By exploiting this vulnerability, attackers could gain a foothold inside servers responsible for processing millions of user requests,” Darius Houle, a security researcher at RunSybil, wrote in a blog post. “They also could strike directly at the underlying cloud infrastructure hosting those workloads.” The researchers demonstrated how a specially crafted model could exploit the flaw to bypass Jinja, a Python-based templating engine used to structure interactions between users and LLMs, sandbox protections, and execute code in the process of serving the model. The attack could expose AI hosting providers that allow customers to upload and run their own models, potentially giving attackers a foothold inside infrastructure processing requests for multiple customers, the post added.

title: OpenSSH flaw lets attackers access password-disabled accounts on some Linux systems
raw_text: A critical vulnerability that affects OpenSSH servers on Linux systems built with the musl C library instead of glibc allows remote attackers to easily bypass authentication and log into accounts that should have password authentication disabled. The flaw impacts the lightweight Alpine Linux, which is widely used for cloud Docker container images, as well as Linux distributions for embedded systems. The security bug, dubbed *SSHole and tracked as CVE-2026-123158 , was discovered by Ozgun Kultekin, a researcher with security testing firm Wakefield, and has existed for the past 10 years. The OpenSSH maintainers moved quickly to add mitigation for the flaw in the OpenSSH 10.6p2 emergency update released Thursday, even though they claim the bug is not actually in their code . “It’s not every day that the ‘exploit’ for a vulnerability in a technology as prevalent as OpenSSH is just ‘send a long password’ or ‘send a lot of A characters,’ but here we are,” said Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at preemptive exposure management firm watchTowr. “On affected systems, the exploit is strikingly simple: send a password between 257 and 1,024 characters long.” Luckily, there are some prerequisites for this exploit to work: The Linux distribution needs to use musl, which means that many popular server distros such as Debian, Ubuntu, and Fedora are not impacted The system needs to use OpenSSH and not alternative SSH server implementations such as Dropbear, which many embedded distros use OpenSSH needs to be configured without support for Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM), the most common Linux login framework OpenSSH needs to allow password-based authentication The attacker needs to know the name of an account for which password login has been disabled at the system level Those conditions are met in default configuration for Alpine Linux and its built-in “alpine” username, which allows executing commands as root. The Alpine project released emergency updates for the openssh package and advises users who can’t update to disable password-based authentication in the OpenSSH configuration and set up key-based authentication. Why the trivial attack works The flaw is the product of three changes made years apart, each solving a different problem. In 2012, musl’s developers capped password length at 256 bytes to stop attackers from tying up server resources by sending long passwords that need to be hashed as part of the login verification process. At the same time they also made the library’s password hashing function return an asterisk (*) whenever it fails. The asterisk is the same character Unix has used since the 1980s to mark accounts for which no password should ever match — accounts with password disabled at the system level. In 2016, OpenSSH changed how it checks passwords for accounts whose own password field offers no salt to hash against, borrowing another account’s salt so that attackers could not guess existing usernames with brute-force login retries and timing the server’s responses. Then in 2022, Alpine switched root’s password field to an asterisk so that SSH key logins would keep working for it. When an attacker sends an over-long password for a password-disabled account on such a system, the hash attempt fails and returns an asterisk, which sshd compares with the asterisk stored in the account’s password field. The two match, and the login succeeds. Alpine Linux cloud images will be the main target Alpine’s standard OpenSSH package is built without PAM, and password logins are enabled by default, so Alpine servers meet the conditions out of the box. On the official cloud images published between versions 3.18.11 and 3.24.3, the default user account, named alpine, is one of the password-disabled accounts, and the images grant it passwordless “doas” privileges. As a result, an attacker who logs in as that user can then switch to root, so the images are exposed as soon as an administrator sets a password for any other account on the system, because a legitimate account with a real password needs to exist for this attack to work. Unlike the critical regreSSHion flaw from 2024 , this one is confined to the musl world, but it requires no exploit engineering of any kind. “Internet-exposed SSH servers are already being hammered by password guesses and brute-force attempts around the clock ,” Knott said. “Exploiting this vulnerability simply means those same attackers add a very long password attempt to that brute-force list. We’d be extremely surprised if we didn’t see SSH brute-forcers attempting this by the weekend.” Organizations should also check whether the flaw was already used against their servers. An “Accepted password” entry in /var/log/messages for an account that has no password, such as root, a key-only user, or the default alpine user, is a strong sign of compromise. Alpine recommends reviewing doas usage, recently created users and files on exposed machines, and its advisory says any server where a login cannot be ruled out should be treated as compromised. Kultekin also published a check script on GitHub that identifies exposed servers and lists the accounts at risk.

title: French banking group hit by supply chain cyberattack
raw_text: French regional banking group Crédit Mutuel Arkéa admitted Wednesday that attackers had accessed an internal account via an unnamed third-party service provider’s platform and transferred funds to other financial institutions. Those funds, it said, could have then been potentially converted to cryptocurrency by the thieves. The day before, cryptocurrency news outlet CoinDesk reported that the attack had been detected on Monday by blockchain investigator ZachXBT , although at the time he did not identify the entity involved. On Wednesday, he identified the suspected victim as Crédit Mutuel Arkéa , which the banking group later confirmed. It did not, however, specify whether the stolen funds were originally in traditional currency or cryptocurrency. This attack comes amidst worries by European regulators about cyber threats to financial institutions as they become more reliant on interconnected systems and external service providers. The bank, which serves the West of France, temporarily suspended some transactions in the wake of the attack to prevent further fraudulent activity. It reported that, as of Wednesday morning, operations were returning to normal after the implementation of additional security controls. French law enforcement is investigating the breach. In its initial announcement, the group reassured customers that their funds were safe. “This incident has no impact on [customer] assets, and has only resulted in a delayed execution of certain transfer operations. Their interests are fully protected, and safeguarding their assets is an absolute priority,” it said. French regional newspaper Le Télégramme reported that the thieves had taken over €118 million (over $133 million); the bank would not confirm the amount but said that the order of magnitude was accurate. The bank said it was still working to assess the precise financial consequences of this attack. “Some of the funds involved have been frozen, and other actions are underway to recover them. While it is therefore still too early to provide a final figure, we can already confirm that the amounts involved are in no way likely to jeopardize the financial health and stability of Crédit Mutuel Arkéa,” it said. The group has 5.8 million customers and manages more than €211 billion (about $237 billion) in assets.

title: Binance heist is stark example of AI governance gaps and basic security failures
raw_text: A chain of avoidable technical and human security failures enabled the largest crypto heist on record, the theft of approximately $6.34 billion from Binance . The improper monitoring and access scoping of an internal AI tool played a major role in helping the hackers, and should serve as a warning for enterprise CISOs to take AI governance seriously. Binance’s initial findings report , published Nov. 3, describes a months-long, multi-stage campaign against its wallet-infrastructure engineers that resulted in malware being installed on developer machines in two separate incidents, only one of which was detected. The attackers were then able to pivot through an internal AI tool to additional developer systems, obtain an access token, and deploy a container on Binance’s infrastructure before executing the rogue withdrawals. While Binance describes this attack as highly sophisticated, there were multiple security failures involved that could have been avoided, from weak or absent access controls to overly broad privileges, poor credential hygiene, and employee security awareness lapses or policy violations. “Developer workstations have quietly become some of the most privileged assets in the enterprise, carrying deployment tokens, signing access, and now AI tools that can act across internal systems on an employee’s behalf,” warns Joe Brinkley, director of offensive security research and community at security firm Cobalt. “Once an attacker controls that machine, an AI tool with broad internal reach becomes one more trusted path they can use.” He adds: “Security teams should treat engineers with production or signing access as a high-value attack surface, test the path from workstation to production the way an adversary would, and scope AI tool permissions as tightly as any service account.” Two compromises, months apart The FBI has attributed the Binance breach to North Korea , identifying the hacking unit as TraderTraitor, which other researchers consider part of the broader Lazarus operation that has stolen billions of dollars from cryptocurrency platforms over the past decade . Binance’s own report relays the FBI’s conclusion and notes that throughout 2026, the company’s security team detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea–linked cyber threat cases. This suggests Binance has the Lazarus APT in its threat model, as it should, and is well aware of the group’s tools, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), which include software supply-chain compromises, the use of malware that masquerades as popular legitimate tools, tricking developers with fake job interviews , and long-horizon social engineering operations. Yet, two Binance engineers fell victim to exactly these tricks, raising questions about the company’s security awareness training as well as its technical controls. In June, a wallet-infrastructure engineer searched the web for a popular AI coding tool and downloaded a tampered Homebrew installer rather than obtaining the software from a trusted source. Homebrew is a package manager and distribution channel for open-source applications on macOS. Binance’s security team detected the anomaly, replaced the device, and rotated all related credentials, but the attackers had already learned who the engineer was and who else worked on the wallet infrastructure team. It’s good that Binance was able to quickly detect the breach, but the incident raises the question of why an engineer was installing software from a search result at all. Does Binance have a policy that employees install software only from approved sources, and is this enforced with technical controls such as application whitelisting? Three months later, the attackers approached a second engineer through a job-hunting platform, posing as a project director recruiting for a company that did not exist. Two staged interviews followed: one with a purported HR representative who shared a social media account filled with personal photos and videos to build trust, and one with someone claiming to be the company’s CEO. At the end of the second interview, the engineer was told to download a coding assignment onto their work computer from a repository. The assignment included malicious code, and this time Binance’s endpoint protection tools did not detect it. The company described this as zero-day malware, but if endpoint protection tools were only capable of detecting known malware, then the whole industry has a problem. Either way, the developer’s actions raise a number of questions regarding security policies, procedures, and awareness at Binance, first among them: Why was the engineer doing job interviews and test assignments on their work computer? Why did they clone a repository directly on their system instead of using a virtual machine? If this is something they regularly do, then it points to lapses in security training or intentional policy violations. And companies cannot solely rely on employees always following policies. They need detection and enforcement mechanisms. “The engineer did multiple things wrong,” says Tim Chase, AVP for cybersecurity at human-risk management company Fable Security. “A modern risk program should have ensured he understood the modern [attack] surface of social engineering that attackers are using today.” Binance did not respond to CSO’s questions on whether it had policies in place that explicitly prohibited the developer’s actions on work computers and whether its employee training covered the fake recruitment social engineering tactic commonly used by North Korean hackers. An overprivileged AI tool enables lateral movement Once the attackers had malware running on the engineer’s computer, they were able to use an internal AI tool present on it to pivot to additional machines belonging to two other engineers from the wallet infrastructure team. Binance did not clarify the purpose of this tool in its report or to CSO, but the fact that it could be used by one compromised user to access different computers suggests its privileges were too broad or that it lacked proper access controls . This is hinted at by the company in its list of remediation steps, which included: “Rebuilt the affected internal AI tool and access controls.” On one of the additional engineering computers, the attackers found a token with permissions to deploy new containers on the company’s infrastructure. Nine days later they used this token on a different compromised engineering computer to deploy a container with a malicious script that interacted with the wallet signing service and initiated withdrawals. This series of events raises additional questions about credential hygiene and access controls because Binance’s report doesn’t describe any additional checks. Why was the token long-lived and not ephemeral for a single operation? Did deployment of containers to production involve additional validation or approval steps? Is there any authentication between the deployed container and the signing service, or was being on the same trusted network enough? Binance did not respond to CSO’s questions about any of these points. “An internal AI tool that can reach engineers’ systems holds the same kind of access as a privileged employee, and most organizations don’t govern it that way,” says Justin Beals, CEO of Strike Graph. “Expect more groups to copy this playbook against anyone holding signing keys, deployment tokens, or production access. Security leaders should treat engineers with production access, and the AI tools those engineers use, as privileged identities. That means restricting what gets installed on work machines, expiring deployment tokens quickly, and logging and reviewing what internal AI tools actually do.” Shlomi Salem, co-founder of Neo, a startup focused on AI agent security, predicted the AI attack vector days before Binance released its findings. “I wouldn’t be surprised if investigators find a poisoned package, a misused agent, or both at the start of this chain,” he said on Oct. 30 after the breach was announced. The takeaway for organizations is that internal AI tools are now part of the attack surface and need to be tested accordingly, Bri Frost, director of product management at Cloud Range, tells CSO. “When an AI tool can reach other systems on an employee’s behalf, an attacker who controls that employee’s machine may inherit everything the tool can do,” she says. “That changes the question security teams need to answer. It’s not only whether the model gives good answers, but what it will do, and for whom, when a request comes from a compromised session.”

The improper monitoring and access scoping of an internal AI tool played a major role in helping the hackers, and should serve as a warning for enterprise CISOs to take AI governance seriously. title: OpenAI built an AI pipeline to find, exploit and patch Linux flaws
raw_text: OpenAI has developed an autonomous AI pipeline that can identify software vulnerabilities, develop working exploits to validate their impact and generate patches for human review. In an October experiment targeting the Linux kernel, the pipeline created exploits for 948 distinct local privilege-escalation (LPE) vulnerabilities at a total API cost of $1.2 million, the company said in a November 4 research report, “ A thousand fewer paths to root .” The system automates vulnerability discovery, dynamic validation, exploit development and patch generation. Human researchers still review the root-cause analysis, proof-of-concept exploits and proposed fixes before findings are reported to maintainers, OpenAI said. The research builds on OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative . Announcing the project in June as part of its Daybreak cybersecurity effort, the company said GPT-5.5 Cyber had identified Linux kernel vulnerabilities and developed 24 LPE exploits. The latest experiment extends that work into a pipeline covering discovery, exploitation and patch generation, the report added. AI changes the economics of vulnerability research The October campaign cost $1,213,430 in API credits, averaging $1,279 per distinct LPE exploit created, OpenAI said. OpenAI compared its research expenditure with historical Linux kernel vulnerability bounty rewards offered by the Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN hacking competitions, which have paid $20,000 to $70,000 for LPE exploits. Based on those numbers, OpenAI estimated the value of the 948 exploits it created at between $18.9 million and $66.3 million, or 16 to 55 times the pipeline’s cost. The comparison does not represent actual bounty payouts or establish that every finding would qualify for those rewards. The latest campaign identified five times more unique LPE vulnerabilities than an earlier experiment using GPT-5.6 Sol, despite three months of additional hardening of the Linux kernel between the scans, OpenAI said. It also reported that its agents used at least 10 novel Linux exploitation techniques based on its analysis of a sample of 166 of the exploits. The pipeline generated candidate patches for the validated vulnerabilities and used iterative testing and variant analysis to improve them, OpenAI said, adding that initial patches sometimes introduced unnecessary code changes or performance trade-offs, or failed to address related vulnerability variants. Humans still needed in the loop While the campaign was going on and before OpenAI could report its results to Linux kernel maintainers, 61 of the vulnerabilities it discovered had already been patched upstream, 43 had staging patches, and another 299 were being publicly discussed. OpenAI said it had submitted hundreds of vulnerability reports and patches to maintainers. The report did not provide a complete remediation breakdown for all 948 findings. The need to validate AI-generated exploits is another brake on reporting. During an early experiment, OpenAI found that 20 of 200 purportedly successful exploits had obtained root privileges by exploiting a different zero-day vulnerability than the one assigned for analysis. The company subsequently introduced additional checks to ensure its AI performed the assigned work. Enterprises evaluating autonomous security tools should demand reproducible exploits, accurate root-cause identification and independent validation, said Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO at Security Brigade. “Achieving a result and correctly explaining how you achieved it are two different things,” he said. Enterprise patching remains a challenge While OpenAI focused on the number of exploits it had found, that’s not the biggest threat, said Sakshi Grover, research director at IDC. “The risk is less the 948 than the length of the window between discovery and fixes reaching production,” she said. An upstream patch does not necessarily mean that the fix has reached the Linux distribution kernel running in an enterprise environment, Grover said. She recommended prioritizing multi-tenant hosts, CI/CD runners, shared bastions, container platforms and developer fleets, and seeking backport timelines from Linux distributors. Thomas Di Giacomo, chief technology and product officer at SUSE, said the company is using similar AI tools to discover and remediate vulnerabilities while working with upstream communities on disclosure and patching. “AI accelerating code analysis and bug hunting represents a fundamental shift in the threat landscape,” Di Giacomo said. He said SUSE’s enterprise Linux security approach combines multiple layers of protection with hardened runtimes for customer applications to mitigate privilege-escalation and container-escape risks. OpenAI added that it plans to extend the research to other critical software projects through Patch the Planet, working with maintainers and security partners on vulnerability discovery, validation and automated patching.

title: OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber ups the ante on vulnerability discovery
raw_text: OpenAI is introducing GPT-6 Cyber, a restricted access model that the company calls its most capable and aligned cybersecurity model yet, “built to help security researchers identify and validate exploitable vulnerabilities, assess their impact, and harden potential patches before they’re released.” OpenAI researchers said they used GPT-6 Cyber to find 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox and develop working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including 588 previously unknown vulnerabilities. Mozilla has begun releasing fixes, and Linux findings are being reported with candidate patches for maintainer review. In a sample of 166 exploits, OpenAI’s researchers identified 10 exploitation techniques that the company says appeared novel, meaning external kernel exploitation experts reportedly had not seen them before, and that could enable someone with local access to obtain root privileges. Highlighting what it called stronger alignment and safeguards, OpenAI said that GPT-6 Cyber “was trained to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately.” In its ExploitGym Honeypot evaluation, the model went beyond the intended scope in only 0.07% of cases, compared with 5.51% for GPT-5.6 Cyber. More bugs, new exploitation paths Chris Hughes, VP of security strategy at Noma Security, believes the Firefox findings suggest a deeper reservoir of vulnerabilities in mature software than defenders may have anticipated. “Mozilla says GPT-6 Cyber surfaced high-severity Firefox bugs after multiple generations of frontier models had already hardened that code,” Hughes told CSO. “If that holds up, the long tail of vulnerabilities in mature software is deeper than most of us assumed, which is the same ‘vulnpocalypse’ pressure many have been discussing this year.” Beyond that, the 10 novel techniques might point to how AI models could not only unearth more vulnerabilities but also create new exploitation paths, according to Rob T. Lee, the new chief AI officer at industrial cybersecurity company Dragos, which recently partnered with OpenAI. “That could mean a few things, but that’s interesting to me as it could reveal models can create new exploitation paths,” Lee told CSO. “Adding new TTPs and exploitation paths will make detection more complex.” (Rob T. Lee just joined Dragos, which is run by company founder and CEO Rob M. Lee.) The promise of security at agent speed During a press call to discuss GPT-6 Cyber, OpenAI’s representatives argued that models can help validate exploitability, investigate alternative attack paths, harden patches, and assist with patch deployment. They described the goal as security operating at “agent speed.” OpenAI researcher Eric Wallace said the goal was to “validate the potential exploitability of vulnerabilities at scale” and prioritize the most consequential flaws. He also emphasized testing fixes against alternative routes of exploitation, noting that “one vulnerability might not be the only attack path.” During the call, OpenAI cybersecurity research lead Clint Gibler touched on advance coordination the company engaged in regarding PHP vulnerabilities with researchers, maintainers, and security vendors. “We wanted to get ahead of that public patch and release, so that as many users and companies could be protected even before the patch was available,” he said. OpenAI worked with Cloudflare “to ensure that they could deploy WAF [web application firewall] rules, which would proactively protect as many websites as possible even before the bug was announced.” Finding flaws is easier to measure than fixing them OpenAI, however, provided no measurements showing how much its models accelerate enterprise patch deployment or reduce exposure. Noma Security’s Hughes argued that defensive applications need more rigorous evaluation, telling CSO, “Detection engineering, incident response, hardening, and prioritization are harder to score because success depends on each organization’s environment, tooling, and risk tolerance.” He believes that sharing defender benchmarks would direct progress toward “the work that closes the remediation gap, not only toward finding more bugs.” Hughes added: “The OpenAI Patch the Planet dashboard currently shows a less than 25% remediation rate thus far, and given the improved finding capability, this is likely to exacerbate that further, meaning more things found but unfixed and likely to be found by malicious actors with similar capabilities or effective harness engineering on sub-tier models. This highlights even further risk for organizations facing the rise of industrialized discovery via AI.” Stronger safeguards, restricted access OpenAI classifies GPT-6 Cyber as “Critical” in cybersecurity under its own Preparedness Framework. “Going out of scope in 0.07% of cases versus 5.51% for the prior model is a real improvement,” Hughes noted. “At the scale these models operate, though, even a small fraction means actions against systems nobody authorized.” OpenAI said that GPT-6 Cyber will initially be available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers, the more permissive of two vetted access tiers in Daybreak, OpenAI’s trusted-access cyber program . (Daybreak Blue is the tier OpenAI recommends for most defenders.) OpenAI said it will progressively expand GPT-6 Cyber access to all Daybreak Red customers over the coming weeks, and is making GPT-5.6 Cyber available to that customer set as well. OpenAI said in briefing materials prior to the press call, “We are working to responsibly expand access to frontier cyber capabilities to many more organizations and members of the security community. To start, we’re broadening access to an alpha of Daybreak Blue for Astra ,” which is OpenAI’s GPT-6 general-purpose frontier model.

title: Teachers surprised pension service not fully returned after migration blackout
raw_text:
The two-week blackout for the switchover of the Teachers’ Pension Scheme from Capita to Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) was not the final stage expected by members, with services still to be brought online.

After three years of build-up and a two-week blackout period, teachers expected the migration to be complete, but there is still work to do, and the process remains “underway”, according to the Department for Education (DfE).

TCS won the 10-year contract in June 2023, replacing Capita, with the takeover set for earlier this month.

While millions of member records were transferred by 2 November as planned, to the surprise of members, critical services are not yet available to them.

A DfE spokesperson said: “Following the planned temporary pause to all teacher pensions services, different elements of the service will come online in a sequenced way.”

But according to former teacher David Fountain, who is supporting teachers who have concerns, this was not explained before. “The ‘sequenced way’ was not detailed before the blackout and had no current publicly explained timeline for what and when is being shared,” he said.

“We were given the impression that it would be fully up and running from day one,” said Fountain, who added that the fact this was not communicated in advance risks causing anxiety among members.

The DfE spokesperson said: “Pension benefits and payments will be paid as usual, and members can visit the Teachers’ Pensions website for the latest updates and urgent support if needed.”

The spokesperson added that the “employer portal is now available for all employers, as well as the contact centre and live chat for members”.

Fountain said the sequenced approach surprise was “akin to being told that a shop will open at 9am and then for everyone getting there for that time, to be told that only staff can go in and it won’t be until midday that they will open doors to customers”.

The DfE was asked by Computer Weekly whether the “sequenced” approach was always part of the plan. The spokesperson said this wouldn’t have been announced in advance.

Computer Weekly asked for details of when different services will go live. The spokesperson said: “[The scheme administrators] will keep members and employers updated every step of the way.”

TCS was contacted for comment but had not responded when this article weas published.

Existing problems

There have been fears over the transfer, following the disastrous Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) migration from MyCSP to Capita. The CSPS contract was originally won by Capita in 2023, around the same time that TCS took the Teachers’ Pension administration contract. It also had a two-year period before the transfer in December 2025, which has been a disaster.

Retired civil servants have been pushed into severe financial hardship due to delays in receiving pensions of almost a year in some cases (see timeline of articles below).

MPs heard last month that some teachers were experiencing problems. In September, amid the fallout of Capita’s botched takeover of the CSPS, a Westminster Hall debate was held where MPs discussed the problems. During the meeting, which was held weeks before the switch from Capita to TCS, Alison Bennet, Liberal Democrat MP for Mid Sussex, said she had been told teachers were experiencing problems with their pensions. She asked: “Are we seeing teachers go through the same ordeal [as civil servants]?

“I have received very concerning casework from teachers in my constituency who seem to be having similar or the same troubles with their pensions,” added Bennet. “The idea that the immense stress and potential financial hardship we’ve heard inflicted on civil servants has been [repeated] with teachers is appalling.”

Comparing the transfer to the Civil Service Pension Scheme supplier switch, Fountain said: “I would say that there are similarities but that we do not have the severity of hardship caused by teachers failing to be paid anything that appears to be the case with the civil service pensions for a large number. However, the issue with data husbandry is, and has been, ongoing.

“Unfortunately, I can see TCS might have similar problems given how many errors are flagged up at the last minute in the process when teachers apply for their pensions,” he added.
