title: Watchdog investigates Europol over ‘irregular’ data processing claims
raw_text:
Europe’s data protection supervisor has confirmed it is conducting a months-long “fact finding” exercise after an investigation by Computer Weekly and partner publications Correctiv and Solomon revealed Europol stored sensitive data for years in a data processing environment that failed to meet European Union (EU) security and data protection standards.

The investigation, based on anonymous testimonies of senior Europol officials and leaked documents, revealed how Europol created a data repository in its Computer Forensics Network (CFN), and used it to store huge volumes of sensitive personal data without full data protection and security safeguards.

Leaked emails have revealed that Europol officials were also aware of the use of a set of tools, known as the Pressure Cooker, set up by Europol’s Internet Referral Unit, for fast-track processing of data scraped from the internet.

The European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) confirmed it was investigating “to decide whether other (and which kind of) supervisory action is necessary” against Europol. It is understood to be focusing on the Pressure Cooker. Previously, the data protection supervisor, Wojciech Wiewiórowski, suggested in a press conference that most of the information revealed by the investigation was not new to the watchdog.

The EDPS has confirmed that Europol has only referred to the Pressure Cooker once in a single document, describing it as the nickname of an existing system. The watchdog has refused to release this document, a Europol ICT 2022 working plan, citing privacy and security exemptions under freedom of information regulations.

Europol claims in a statement published on its website that allegations that it used a processing environment outside the requirements of EU law and data protection rules were “incorrect”. It said it “proactively engaged” with the European Data Protection Supervisor over the compliance of its IT systems.

Former Europol officials said Europol’s decision to proactively expose compliance issues in 2019 was a damage control manoeuvre taken by the then incoming executive director of the agency, Catherine De Bolle, who did not want to inherit the liabilities identified in Europol’s CFN data storage network. De Bolle, Europol executive director at the time, declined to be interviewed, and left the position in May 2026.

Significant questions remain unanswered over the lack of data protection and security safeguards in Europol’s data network. As reported in internal Europol monitoring documents, by 2019, the CFN had severe security vulnerabilities including insufficient logging of administrative actions, the lack of a reliable mechanism to track who had accessed or modified sensitive data, unrestricted software installation, and a lack of effective password management.

Information stored in the CFN included phone records, financial transactions, geolocation data and identity documents – belonging in many cases to individuals who had never been suspected of any crime.

In February 2026, Wiewiórowski informed the Joint Parliamentary Scrutiny Group that the watchdog was closing its years-long monitoring of Europol’s irregular big data repositories – even though 15 of its 150 recommendations had not been implemented. The outstanding items, the EDPS noted, included matters of “particular importance”, including core security measures for the CFN.

In a separate response to written questions by MEP Saskia Bricmont in May, Europol disclosed that the EDPS had resolved only three of the 10 recommendations related to CFN. “For the other seven recommendations, specific safeguards have been taken forward and additional work is in progress,” Europol said.

This echoed the findings of Europol’s internal 2019 mitigation task force, which reported that the CFN was unfixable and that certain issues would be resolved only when Europol migrated its repository of data to a planned replacement system, which has yet to be fully delivered.

Europol said in a statement it would implement the seven remaining recommendations by migrating to a new IT environment, known as the New Forensic Environment.

“Much of this migration has already been completed, with four of the original 25 Analysis Projects still to transfer,” it said. “Their migration is scheduled for the first quarter of 2027, allowing the remaining recommendations to be fully implemented and the CFN to be decommissioned. Safeguards have been taken forward in the meantime.”

Europol published a statement on its website stating that the claims made in the investigation “are incorrect and are based on a misunderstanding of Europol’s operational setup and legal framework”. 

Additional reporting by Lydia Emmanouilidou

Questions over the Pressure Cooker persist

In a statement in July, Europol gave the following explanation about the Pressure Cooker:

  • “The term ‘Pressure Cooker’, sometimes used in this context, is an internal ICT project management term referring to the acquisition, adaptation or development of digital tools and solutions to respond rapidly to business needs, while remaining compliant even with evolving operational requirements.
  • “Since 2017, the term has been used for specific online tools and digital solutions supporting the IRU’s [Internet Referral Unit’s] work to identify relevant online information in accordance with the principles of necessity and proportionality.”

From 2017 onwards, based on its legal framework, Europol had an obligation to request a prior consultation for new processing capabilities from EDPS.

Asked why such a consultation was not sought out by the agency, Europol responded: “We didn’t state that the Pressure Cooker was used since 2017, but that the term ‘Pressure Cooker’ has been used since 2017.”

The police agency said the use of the term did not mark the introduction of a new processing capability, and that the underlying processing environment was part of Europol’s Internet Facing Operational Environment, which was already established in 2015.

“The activities were already subject to data protection supervision, including an inspection by the Joint Supervisory Body in 2016,” it said.

“The Europol Regulation only became applicable in May 2017, introducing EDPS supervision and prior consultation requirements for qualifying new processing operations and substantial changes to existing systems,” Europol added. “It did not require retroactive consultation of already established processing operations.

“Specific components of Europol’s internet-facing environment have since undergone EDPS prior consultation, and Europol continues to work with the supervisor on implementing its opinion and on future initiatives requiring consultation,” it said.

Europol claims the processing environment under the term “Pressure Cooker” had not undergone any substantial changes since from the introduction of EDPS supervision in May 2017 until October 2025. In that month, Europol requested a prior consultation for a processing environment named the Internet Facing Operational Environment – Quick Response Area.

However, a trove of heavily redacted internal emails discussing technical issues related to IFOE and the Pressure Cooker, obtained through an access to document request and spanning from 2017 to 2024, suggests the processing environment was undergoing constant development.

One email from July 2024, states that “[the] internet is a fast evolving environment and we need to constantly adapt our toolset to the terrorist modus operandi evolution. A clearer example of that could be that we have completely changed our toolset every three years since 2016”.

title: Cutting cloud carbon: From accounting to action
raw_text:
IT operator infrastructure strategies depend on cloud services for some or all of their IT operations. Meanwhile, public cloud use will grow as AI adoption expands to augment and drive enterprise and government IT workloads. And so, operators should account for and establish reduction goals for the greenhouse gas emissions associated with these operations. 

Operators have this responsibility because they select the location(s) where they will deploy workloads and the type, size, and work capacity of CPU cores, GPUs, memory modules, and storage devices on which they are hosted. 

They also control infrastructure utilisation through the management strategies and operating systems under which they deploy their workloads. The efficiency of a public cloud datacentre, as measured by a metric based on work delivered per unit of energy consumed, depends on how efficiently users deploy and execute their workloads.

To optimise this metric, users must operate workloads as efficiently as possible, and minimise energy use and GHG emissions. While emissions are accounted for in Scope 3, operators can calculate reasonable GHG emissions estimates, and in some cases energy use estimates, by using calculators offered by cloud providers or open source tools such as Cloud Carbon Footprint. The ability to develop a reasonable estimate of these values enables operators to take responsibility for and set energy use and carbon emissions reduction goals for their operations. 

Cloud providers should deliver highly efficient facilities and IT infrastructure where customers can deploy and run their IT workloads. They should report the emissions associated with these operations as Scope 2 and pass those emissions to their customers as Scope 3. They are also responsible for Scope 3 emissions associated with the facility and IT infrastructure materials and equipment (controlled by the cloud provider), and for planning their eventual reduction (in collaboration with their suppliers).

Given this complex interaction between IT operators and their cloud service providers, many operators believe cloud providers are the party responsible for accounting for and reducing GHG emissions. In reality, IT operators play an important role in efficiently operating IT infrastructure and taking steps to minimise energy use and emissions through site selection and workload placement, while recognising the geographical limits imposed by response time and reliability requirements. 

Reduction of operational emissions

Each operator should set utilisation and operational goals that minimise IT infrastructure resource use and energy use and reduce associated carbon emissions. One goal should be a three- to five-year energy-use and emissions reduction target that supports achieving a net-zero-emissions cloud infrastructure by a specific future date. 

To achieve the necessary emissions reductions, a strategy must be established with three key components: 

  • Minimise the energy use of current operations, 

  • Optimise the operation of new workloads at inception, and; 

  • Locate the workloads at the most carbon-efficient location(s) that meet the workload response time and reliability needs. 

The discussion of GHG emissions management is facility-focused and is based on location-based, not market-based, accounting. An IT operator should focus on decarbonising the energy supply that powers their infrastructure without relying on offsets.   

Minimise the emissions of existing operations

Many operators select cloud infrastructure capability and capacity to match the expected demand and operational requirements of their IT workloads. Once they are deployed, they track peak loads, response time, and other key operational metrics to ensure customer needs are met while ignoring utilisation metrics. 

Actively managing infrastructure capacity and utilisation can have huge returns.  

Discussions with companies that offer capacity and utilisation tracking and optimisation services indicate that operators who right-size CPU and memory infrastructure and maximise its utilisation can achieve significant cost savings and reduce energy use and associated carbon emissions by up to 40%. This strategy offers a direct path to reductions that will make significant contributions toward an interim carbon reduction or net zero goal.

Energy savings and emissions reductions can also be achieved by deploying workloads to next-generation infrastructure. An IT operator should regularly review their cloud provider's infrastructure offerings and move to more efficient work-per-watt systems as they are deployed and where it makes business sense. 

These operational reductions can be documented and validated by capturing before-and-after measurements of energy use and emissions quantities. Documentation should include changes in purchased infrastructure capacity and before-and-after energy use (where available) and emissions quantities. 

Optimise infrastructure for new workload deployments

IT operators should have a standard workload deployment process that includes pre-testing workloads to determine the CPU-to-memory ratio that optimises infrastructure performance and utilisation while minimising energy use. The process should also periodically recheck that ratio and infrastructure utilisation to reallocate workloads and infrastructure to maintain performance and efficiency. The process to document and validate reductions described above should be used when re-allocation is performed.

Operators should catalogue and publicise energy and emissions reductions in their annual environmental report. Reductions are reported on a project basis and can be contextualised as percentage reductions against the cloud operation’s current annual total or baseline year energy use and emissions. A baseline is not necessarily required, as the ultimate goal is to power the infrastructure with carbon-free energy (CFE).

Utilising carbon-free energy 

Datacentre systems run on electrical power. So, the final step in decarbonising public cloud operations requires that hosting datacentre(s) maximise CFE consumption and have a plan to increase the percentage of CFE used over time. 

Site selection is a critical step in managing GHG emissions from public cloud deployments. Each facility has an associated electricity emissions factor based on the contracted, on-site, and grid-based generation that supplies energy to the site. That factor will change monthly (the typical emissions reporting period for public cloud providers) based on the season, weather conditions, and grid performance. For a given geographical area, some facilities may have a lower emissions factor and a better plan/outlook for further reduction. The facility emissions factor should be part of the procurement criteria, though other factors like IT performance and cost are likely to predominate in facility selection. 

Operators can consider carbon-aware workload placement software for non-critical workloads or time-insensitive batch jobs. Most available software systems are in early-stage development, not widely proven, and not widely deployed. These systems offer a means to achieve further emissions reductions, but their immaturity introduces unattractive operational risk and limits their usefulness. 

Managing material and equipment embedded emissions 

Public cloud service providers are responsible for design, construction, and material and equipment procurement for their datacentres. They set procurement specifications and can collaborate on developing low-carbon materials, such as concrete and steel. While many initiatives are underway to develop low-carbon materials, to achieve volume production and incorporate them into equipment is a decades-long process. Because they hold relationships with suppliers, cloud providers should account for, report, and manage reduction efforts with their suppliers for these materials. 

Accounting for these Scope 3 emissions offers IT operators little actionable value. They do not control facility procurement or supplier decisions, and providers often report emissions before operators contract for infrastructure. While some individuals and groups have advocated for “depreciating” Scope 3 emissions, this practice gives operators no actionable data and adds complexity that only confuses emissions reporting.  

Reducing cloud emissions will be a journey 

Datacentres depend on electrical power. In almost all cases, an electricity grid carries a carbon emissions factor. Only two major geographical regions, Latin America (65%) and Europe (71%), supply more than 50% CFE in their grid networks. The Middle East has the lowest percentage at 8%. Decarbonising datacentre operations will require continuing efforts to develop and deploy CFE generation sources and energy storage systems. 

Reducing public cloud emissions is a shared responsibility. IT operators must act on the operations they control. That means right-sizing IT resources, improving resource utilisation, and selecting locations supplied by low carbon electricity where performance and reliability constraints allow. 

Cloud providers must improve infrastructure efficiency, decarbonise electricity supplies, and work with their suppliers to address embedded emissions from materials and equipment. Emissions estimates need not be perfect to support these actions, but claimed reductions should be backed by documented and validated before-and-after energy use and GHG emissions estimates. 

The priority is to connect carbon accounting to operational decisions, rather than treat reporting as an end in itself. Operators should establish reduction goals, validate and report project-level results for their IT infrastructure, and assess and support cloud providers’ progress toward carbon-free energy and low-carbon materials. Focusing on these practical steps gives operators a path to reducing the GHG emissions associated with their cloud operations.

Jay Dietrich is research director for energy and sustainability at the Uptime Institute

summary:
IT operator infrastructure strategies depend on cloud services for some or all of their IT operations. Meanwhile, public cloud use will grow as AI adoption expands to augment and drive enterprise and government IT workloads. And so, operators should account for and establish reduction goals for the greenhouse gas emissions associated with these operations. 

Operators have this responsibility because they select the location(s) where they will deploy workloads and the type, size, and work capacity of CPU cores, GPUs, memory modules, and storage devices on which they are hosted. 

They also control infrastructure utilisation through the management strategies and operating systems under which they deploy their workloads. The efficiency of a public cloud datacentre, as measured by a metric based on work delivered per unit of energy consumed, depends on how efficiently users deploy and execute their workloads.

To optimise this metric, users must operate workloads as efficiently as possible, and minimise energy use and GHG emissions.

title: Zurich uncovers £19m of fraud with Quantexa data analytics
raw_text:
Zurich UK has discovered £109.3m worth of fraud over the past year using data analytics technology from Quantexa.

The insurer has deployed the technology over the past year, exposing the work of criminal gangs involved in so-called crash-for-cash scams and other fraudulent schemes.

Scott Clayton, head of claims fraud at Zurich UK and chair of the Insurance Fraud Bureau (IFB), said: “Insurance fraud in the UK is becoming more sophisticated, more organised and increasingly technology-enabled. Criminal networks are constantly adapting their tactics, whether that’s staged accidents, ghost broking, fabricated claims or the use of AI-generated evidence.”

Ghost broking is a technique and practice whereby fraudsters pose as bona fide brokers to sell car insurance policies that are fake or invalid.

Clayton added: “The £109m of fraud we’ve uncovered this year shows both the scale of the threat and the importance of staying ahead of it. Connected data is transforming the fight against fraud, helping us expose hidden relationships, identify organised networks and protect honest customers from footing the bill for criminal activity. The combination of advanced analytics, specialist investigators and human judgement is proving a powerful defence against a rapidly evolving threat.

“We’re the first insurer in the UK to use technology that brings together information from Companies House, Equifax, industry intelligence and the Insurance Fraud Register to give us a much richer picture across every claim. That helps us identify crucial connections and information that might otherwise be difficult to spot.”

Quantexa and Zurich calculate the volume of fraud as equivalent to one claim every two hours.

They claim Zurich has uncovered a fraud network involving more than 90 UK claims, where drivers were deliberately targeted on roundabouts, with fraudsters exploiting blind spots and lane changes to cause collisions.

They said the fraudsters deliberately caused more than 100 accidents, creating claims worth over £1m.

Quantexa’s AI and advanced analytics software is said to have helped identify 860 fraudulent claims worth £17.9m, amounting to one in five of the fraud cases.

Zurich found 4,359 fraudulent claims across its casualty, motor and property categories. The number of fraudulent claims identified has risen by 22% from 3,562 in 2022 to 4,359 in the last year, it said.

The Quantexa technology has revealed links between suspicious claims and a common accident location, claimants using aliases to conceal previous activity, and organised fraud involving professional enablers such as rogue solicitors and accident management companies.

The platform is also said to have helped investigators identify people living in one part of the UK who were linked to suspected staged accidents hundreds of miles away. 

Vishal Marria, founder and CEO of Quantexa, said: “Fraud hides in the gaps between claims, which is why seeing the full context matters. By putting every claim in context, networks come into view, organised threats are stopped earlier, and genuine claims are dealt with more quickly.”

Ursula Jallow, executive director of the IFB, said: “Insurance fraud is becoming increasingly sophisticated and AI-driven, making it vital that we continue to invest in the systems, controls and partnerships needed to protect businesses and consumers.”

Zurich’s is not the only set of use cases for this technology. In 2023, the government’s Public Sector Fraud Authority (PSFA), which is part of the Cabinet Office and HM Treasury, signed a £4m deal with Quantexa to use artificial intelligence to find potential fraudsters.

And the advanced analytics supplier is one of a cohort popular with senior civil servants and politicians moving to the private sector. Computer Weekly counted four of 63 personnel moves between the public sector and 20 IT, cloud and AI suppliers from 2010 to 2026 as being to Quantexa.
